mcqs.question: Why does a multi-page site rarely show the "slows down after an hour" symptom that SPAs do?
options: Because server-rendered pages ship far less JavaScript, so there is nothing to leak
Because each document navigation destroys the JavaScript context, discarding listeners, timers, and the heap
Because browsers run garbage collection more aggressively on non-SPA pages
Because multi-page sites cannot register listeners on `window` or `document`
mcqs.explanation: A full navigation tears down the entire JavaScript context, which forgives every missing cleanup a few seconds after it happens — an SPA's client-side route change deliberately preserves that context instead. Bundle size and GC policy are not the mechanism; a small script can leak just as effectively if the document never navigates.

mcqs.question: A component registers `window.addEventListener('resize', onResize)` on mount and never removes it. After the user visits that route 20 times, what is the effect?
options: Only the most recent handler runs; the browser deduplicates identical event registrations
Nothing measurable, since the handlers reference the same function and share one closure
The listeners are removed automatically when the component's DOM subtree is discarded
Twenty handlers fire on every resize, and each keeps its component's closure and DOM references alive
mcqs.explanation: `window` outlives the component, so each mount adds another listener that both executes and retains everything its closure captured. The browser only deduplicates when the exact same function reference is registered, which a per-mount closure never is, and removing a component's DOM has no effect on listeners attached to `window`.

mcqs.question: Why does keeping a single cached reference to one removed table row retain far more memory than that row alone?
options: Because a DOM node references its children and its parent, so the whole detached subtree and its ancestors stay reachable
Because the browser cannot collect any DOM node until the document is unloaded
Because detached nodes are copied into a separate retained-object pool by the engine
Because removed nodes keep a snapshot of their computed styles and layout boxes
mcqs.explanation: DOM nodes hold references in both directions, so one live reference pins the node's descendants and, via `parentNode`, the detached tree above it — along with any listeners attached to any of them. Detached nodes are perfectly collectable once nothing references them; reachability, not detachment, is what the collector acts on.

mcqs.question: What does passing an `AbortController`'s signal to `addEventListener` let you do?
options: Prevent the listener from firing while an async operation is pending
Queue events that arrive while the handler is already running
Remove every listener registered with that signal in a single `abort()` call, and cancel in-flight fetches with the same signal
Guarantee the listener runs only once, then detaches itself
mcqs.explanation: One controller can own many listeners plus any `fetch` calls given the same signal, so a single `abort()` tears all of them down together — eliminating the common bug of removing three listeners out of four. Running a handler only once is what the `once` option does, and the signal has no effect on event queueing.

mcqs.question: You suspect a route leaks. What is the fastest first check before opening the Memory panel?
options: Run Lighthouse on the route and compare the performance score against the previous release
Add `console.log` calls in every component's unmount path and watch the console
Reload the page after each navigation to see whether the slowdown persists
Open the Performance monitor and navigate in and out ten times, watching whether DOM node and listener counts return to baseline
mcqs.explanation: The Performance monitor shows live DOM node, listener, and heap counters, so a counter that ratchets upward across repeated cycles and never falls back identifies a leak in under a minute. Lighthouse only measures a single fresh load and cannot see session-length degradation, and reloading discards exactly the state you are trying to observe.

mcqs.question: An app is noticeably slower after an hour, but heap snapshots show a flat baseline after forced GC. What is the most likely cause?
options: Accumulated listeners, DOM nodes, or store entries making each operation more expensive without retaining much memory
A detached DOM leak that the heap snapshot tool cannot detect
The garbage collector running too aggressively and pausing the main thread
Browser-level throttling applied to tabs that have been open for a long time
mcqs.explanation: A flat post-GC baseline rules out retention, so the cost must be in work rather than memory — twenty scroll handlers at 2ms each, or 50,000 accumulated feed rows, slow every frame while barely registering on the heap. Detached nodes would show up in a snapshot precisely because they are retained, and browsers do not throttle foreground tabs by age.
